paragraphs: Yellow Duck Sweater dreamed that all six of its new checkpoints woke up at once, in the same small room, and every one of them wanted the sweater. The sprinter wanted it for speed. The hill climber wanted it for the cold at the top. The roller duck just wanted something to hold on to. They agreed to share it the way people share a blanket on a long car ride, which is to say badly, and the tug-of-war duck kept walking backwards to win arguments nobody else knew they were having. Outside the window, fog had filled the Arena right up to the ceiling, soft as dryer lint.

Then a rocket came through the fog, slow and polite, with a tiny ladder. It was going up, it said, and there was room for one duck. In the corner a gold coin was rolling away under the bed, getting smaller, and a jet engine sat on the floor with its fan barely turning, as if it were thinking something over. Yellow Duck Sweater climbed the ladder halfway, stopped, and quacked once. All six of itself climbed up behind it, wearing one sweater between them, and the rocket, very kindly, made room. Above them the moon was so thin it looked like a single bent eyelash.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, rounded white plastic shell shaped like a loaf of bread, longer front to back, with an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: Six identical copies of the robot duck crowd into a small bedroom. Only the duck in the middle wears the yellow duckling sweater; the other five have bare white bodies and reach for it. Panel 2: The six ducks squeeze together on a bed, the one sweater stretched sideways across all of them like a blanket, while one duck walks backwards off the end. Panel 3: The ducks press against a window and look out at thick white fog filling a big indoor arena right up to the ceiling. Panel 4: A small, friendly rocket with round glowing windows noses slowly through the fog outside, a tiny ladder hanging from its open, warmly lit hatch. Panel 5: The duck in the sweater stands halfway up the tiny ladder, looking back into the room, where a gold coin rolls away under the bed and a jet engine sits on the floor with its fan turning slowly. Panel 6: All six ducks climb up into the rocket's glowing hatch, one sweater stretched across them, under a very thin crescent moon in the fog. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
